title: Emraan Hashmi Wipes the Frost Off the Glass — and Bollywood Horror Has Its King Back
excerpt: After five years away, the genre's most recognisable face headlines 'Rooh', a musical-horror spectacle from the 'Breathe' director, dropping in three languages in 2027.
body:
The poster opens in a frost-bitten forest, a girl's body hanging weightless in the air, and then a hand wipes the rime off a pane of glass to reveal a pair of eyes you'd know anywhere. They belong to Emraan Hashmi — and just like that, the man who scared a generation half to death is back where he belongs.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=R2BDW7IZVd4

After five years away from the genre, Hashmi has signed on to headline Rooh, a self-styled "musical-horror spectacle" unveiled on June 23 with a motion poster that Vicked Films Productions dropped across social media with a single, gloriously ominous line: "You won't see it coming. You will feel it forever." It is exactly the kind of tagline that gets screenshotted at 2 a.m. and shared into a hundred diaspora WhatsApp groups before sunrise.

"ROOH is a film that immediately connected with me because it brings together new-age horror, emotion and music in a very powerful way. This is a space that audiences have always associated with me, and the world Mayank is creating feels intense, emotional and cinematic." — Emraan Hashmi

He isn't wrong about the association. For a certain kind of viewer — the ones who grew up renting VCDs of Raaz: The Mystery Continues and gasping through Raaz 3 — Hashmi is Bollywood horror. He gave the genre its swagger, its slow-burn dread, and more than a few of its most quotable melodies. Ek Thi Daayan in 2013 leaned into the eerie elegance; the 2021 misfire Dybbuk went straight to OTT amid the pandemic and quietly vanished. Since then he's been off chasing thrillers and antiheroes. Rooh is the homecoming the fanbase has been not-so-quietly demanding.

What makes this one worth the curiosity is who's behind the camera. Mayank Sharma — the creator-director of Prime Video's slick, sweaty Breathe franchise — knows how to build tension that gets under your skin and stays there. He's co-writing with Vishal Kapoor, whose credits include the genuinely unnerving Lapachhapi and the Chhorii universe, which is to say: this is not a couple of amateurs chasing a jump-scare paycheck. These are people who treat fear as architecture.

"ROOH is my attempt to create a film that goes beyond fear. It's emotionally layered, immersed with an unsettling atmosphere, and presented with contemporary cinematic treatment. I'm thrilled to collaborate with Emraan for this deeply layered character." — Mayank Sharma, director

The "musical" part is the gamble — and the seduction. Hashmi's horror peak was inseparable from its soundtracks; half the reason Raaz 3 lodged in the national memory was its chart-conquering songs. Folding music into the scare architecture isn't a gimmick for him, it's a return to formula, updated for a generation raised on atmospheric horror like Tumbbad and Stree. Done well, it could be spine-chilling. Done badly, it could be a karaoke night in a haunted house. The motion poster — with its levitating figure, its creeping musical score, its single icy reveal — suggests the makers are aiming for the former, and aiming high. Industry sources say an international crew is involved, with the emphasis squarely on scale and visual finesse.

Here's the part the diaspora will actually clock: Rooh is being built as a theatrical event, releasing in 2027 in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu simultaneously. That three-language strategy is now the default for any Indian film with global ambitions, and it's good news for NRI audiences in the US, UK, Canada and the Gulf, where pan-Indian releases increasingly land in local multiplexes on opening weekend. A horror film with a built-in nostalgia hook and a multilingual footprint is precisely the kind of title that travels — expect it to turn up at AMC and Cineworld screens wherever there's a desi catchment, and on a major streamer not long after.

And Hashmi isn't slowing down in the meantime. Before Rooh materializes, he'll surface in Awarapan 2, the long-awaited sequel to the 2007 cult favorite, this time helmed by Nitin Kakkar and co-starring Randeep Hooda, Disha Patani and Shabana Azmi. The serial-kisser-turned-character-actor is having the kind of mid-career renaissance most stars would sell their souls for.

But it's Rooh that has the genre faithful genuinely buzzing. A horror icon, a director who knows dread, a 2027 release built for the big screen and three languages — the casting alone makes this a must-watch. Whether it lives up to that frost-covered first look is two years away. For now, the eyes in the poster are doing exactly what they were always so good at: refusing to look away.
